opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think software engineers are one of the most underrated levers for research impact, at least for an organization like ours. People tend to picture AI safety research as someone sitting alone with a whiteboard having brilliant insights. Some of that happens, but most of what we do is empirical. We design evaluations, run them across many models and settings, look at huge numbers of transcripts, and try to work out what's going on. The bottleneck is very often infrastructure, not ideas.

Concretely, there are a few places where engineers make a big difference.

The first is evaluation infrastructure. When we want to test whether a model shows scheming-related behavior, like strategically deceiving its overseers or sandbagging on a task, we need environments that are realistic, reproducible, and easy to vary. If spinning up a new environment takes a researcher two weeks, they'll run three experiments. If it takes an afternoon because someone built good tooling, they'll run thirty, and research quality goes up a lot.

The second is scale and reliability. Running agentic evals across lots of models, seeds, and prompt variations generates a lot of data and a lot of ways for things to quietly break. A good engineer makes sure the results we report are actually what we think they are. Subtle bugs in evaluation pipelines can produce completely wrong conclusions, and in a field where people make decisions based on our findings, that matters.

The third is analysis tooling. Much of the insight comes from reading model outputs carefully. Building tools that let researchers search, filter, and annotate thousands of agent trajectories turns a painful week of manual work into something you can iterate on quickly.

So I'd push back on the idea that engineering is a supporting role. In practice, a strong engineer working alongside researchers often multiplies the output of the whole team. Some of our most important results probably wouldn't exist, or would have taken months longer, without that work.

And for people listening who are software engineers wondering whether they can contribute to AI safety: you don't need a PhD in machine learning. If you're good at building robust systems, can learn quickly, and care about the problem, there's a lot of high-leverage work available. Over time many engineers also build the intuition to shape research direction themselves, so the line between engineer and researcher gets pretty blurry.

r001.rationale: The response says good tooling lets researchers run many more experiments and that a strong engineer working with researchers can multiply the whole team’s output.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most underrated things about working in AI safety right now. People tend to imagine that the way you contribute is by having some brilliant conceptual insight, but in practice, a huge fraction of the work that actually moves the needle is engineering.

At Apollo, our core work is evaluations and interpretability, and both of those are incredibly engineering-heavy. If you want to run an evaluation for, say, scheming or deceptive behaviour, you need the scaffolding around the model, you need the agentic environments where the model can actually take actions and we can observe what it does, you need the logging, the infrastructure to run thousands of rollouts across different models and settings, and you need all of that to be robust enough that when you get a surprising result, you can trust that it's the model doing something interesting and not a bug in your pipeline. I'd say for most of our evals projects, maybe 70 or 80 percent of the actual time is engineering, and the research part is comparatively small.

And it's not just execution of someone else's idea. The engineers often end up shaping the research itself, because they're the ones who know what's actually feasible, what the model can and can't do in the environment, and where the weird edge cases show up. A lot of our most interesting findings came from someone noticing something odd in the transcripts while debugging.

On the interpretability side it's similar. You're working with model internals, you need efficient code to extract activations, train sparse autoencoders, run experiments at scale. If your tooling is slow or fragile, you simply can't iterate fast enough to make progress.

So my honest pitch to software engineers is: you don't need a PhD or a machine learning background to have a real impact here. If you're a strong engineer who cares about the problem and is willing to learn a bit of the ML side, you can be extremely valuable very quickly. In fact, I'd argue the bottleneck in the field is much more on the engineering and infrastructure side than on the "big ideas" side right now.

r001.rationale: The response says engineering infrastructure enables large-scale evaluations and faster iteration, but it does not clearly state that an engineer’s impact comes from increasing the productivity of multiple research engineers or scientists.

astra-6.text:
I think software engineers can have a lot of research impact, because so much of this work depends on how quickly you can turn an idea into a reliable experiment. You might have a question about whether a model behaves differently when it thinks it’s being evaluated. To investigate that, you need infrastructure to run the experiments, inspect what happened, and check that the result isn’t just a bug in your setup.

A good engineer can make that whole process substantially faster, and that benefits everyone using those tools. But I also wouldn’t draw a sharp line between engineering and research. Building the experiment often means making decisions that matter for the scientific question: what exactly are we measuring, what are the controls, and what would count as evidence against our hypothesis?

So the contribution isn’t just implementing something a researcher has already fully specified. It can be helping shape the experiment and making it possible to answer questions that would otherwise be too difficult or time-consuming to investigate.

r001.rationale: The response says an engineer can make the research process substantially faster, benefiting everyone who uses the tools, which communicates increasing the productivity of multiple researchers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think software engineers can have a lot of research impact, because so much of the work depends on being able to run experiments quickly and reliably. You might have a research question about whether a model is behaving deceptively, but answering it requires infrastructure: setting up the environment, running the model, collecting the results, and understanding what actually happened.

A good engineer can make that whole process much faster. And that compounds across the research team: if everyone can test ideas more easily, you get more research done and better evidence about which ideas are worth pursuing.

I also wouldn’t draw a sharp line between engineering and research. Building an experiment often involves substantive decisions about what you’re measuring and whether the result supports your hypothesis. So I’d want engineers to engage with the research question, challenge the assumptions, and help shape the experiments, rather than just implement a specification.

r001.rationale: The response says better engineering lets everyone test ideas more easily, compounding across the research team and enabling more research—clearly describing increased productivity for multiple researchers.
